title: Philosophical and Scientific Influences on the Halakhic Writings of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas and His Circle
content:
Philosophical and Scientific Influences on the Halakhic Writings of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas and His Circle
Introduction: Rabbi Hasdai Crescas – Philosopher and Halakhic Decisor
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (acronym Rahak, c. 1340 – 1410/1411) stands as one of the most complex and influential figures in medieval Jewish thought. His intellectual enterprise presents a unique combination of two fields that seem, on the face of it, to be opposed: on the one hand, he is considered one of the most profound and innovative Jewish philosophers, whose book "Or Hashem" ("The Light of the Lord") poses a trenchant challenge to the Aristotelian tradition; on the other hand, he was a Torah scholar and a leading halakhic decisor in Spain of the late 14th and early 15th centuries. Examining his halakhic writings is not merely a biographical supplement but an essential strategic move for understanding his intellectual enterprise as a whole, since it reveals the way in which his philosophical conceptions shaped his approach to the central source of authority in the life of the Jewish community.
Crescas acquired his Torah and philosophical education from his grandfather, after whom he was named, and from one of the greatest scholars of the generation, Rabbi Nissim Gerondi (the Ran), in Barcelona. His standing as a leader was established with the founding of study houses in Barcelona and Saragossa; he served as a halakhic adviser to the sages of his generation, among them the Rivash, and nurtured disciples who became important Talmud commentators, such as Rabbi Yosef Chaviva.
Paradoxically, despite his exalted standing and his declared aspiration to compose a comprehensive halakhic code that would compete with Maimonides' "Mishneh Torah" and offer an alternative to it, not a single halakhic book of his has survived. All that remains of his vast halakhic enterprise is a few isolated remnants, which allow only a partial glimpse into his rich world.
The present study rests on three halakhic fragments of his that have survived:
His critique of Maimonides' principles of codification, which appears in the introduction to his book "Or Hashem".
A brief discussion of the laws of Passover, incorporated into his Passover sermon – the only sermon of his that has survived.
A halakhic responsum by his disciple, Rabbi Yosef Albo, setting out his teacher's ruling on the question of the "lethal woman" (isha katlanit).
This article will argue that an analysis of Albo's responsum and of the other remnants of Crescas's halakhic writing reveals a consistent intellectual approach, one that challenges the labelling of Crescas as an anti-rationalist. We shall see how Crescas did not reject science and philosophy but systematically harnessed them as indispensable working tools within the field of halakha, thereby offering a unique model of integration between Torah and wisdom. To appreciate the depth of his innovation, one must first examine the halakhic background of the question of the katlanit as it had developed up to his time.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. The Halakhic Background: The Prohibition of the "Lethal Woman" up to Crescas's Time
Understanding the halakhic development of the law of the "lethal woman" before Crescas's period is a necessary condition for appreciating the originality of his approach. Only against the background of the interpretive tradition that crystallized around this question can one identify the innovation in his incorporation of philosophical-scientific considerations into his rulings, and the way in which he builds an additional storey on the traditional discussion without undermining its foundations.
The source of the prohibition lies in a Talmudic discussion in Tractate Yevamot, where a central Amoraic dispute arises concerning the cause of death of the husbands of such a woman. The dispute revolves around two opposing approaches to understanding the phenomenon:
The approach of Rav Huna: "the source causes" (ma'ayan gorem). According to this approach, the cause of the husbands' death is biological-medical, connected with a disease transmitted through sexual contact. "Ma'ayan" ("source", "spring") is a euphemism for the woman's womb.
The approach of Rav Ashi: "fortune causes" (mazal gorem). This approach attributes the cause of death to an astrological factor, that is, to the woman's "bad" fate, which is determined by the system of the stars.
The central Talmudic text presents the dispute as follows:
Amar leh Rav Mordechai le-Rav Ashi: hakhi amar Avimi me-Hagronia mi-shmeh de-Rav Huna: ma'ayan gorem, ve-Rav Ashi amar: mazal gorem. Mai beinaihu? Ika beinaihu de-arsah u-meit, i nami de-nafal mi-dikla u-meit.
Translation: Rav Mordechai said to Rav Ashi: Thus said Avimi of Hagronia in the name of Rav Huna: the source causes [the death of the woman's husbands], and Rav Ashi said: the [woman's] fortune caused [the death of her husbands]. What [is the practical difference] between them? There is [a difference] between them where he betrothed her and died [before the marriage]. Likewise [there is a difference] where [the husband] fell from a palm tree and died.
(Tractate Yevamot, 64b)
Each approach has clear practical implications: according to Rav Huna, if the husband died after the betrothal but before the marriage, or if he died in an accident ("fell from a palm tree"), there is no reason to forbid the woman to marry again. According to Rav Ashi, by contrast, the prohibition applies in every case, since the death is connected with the woman's fate and not with its circumstances. The overwhelming majority of the sages of medieval Spain adopted Rav Ashi's approach and regarded "fortune" (mazal) as the decisive factor.
Despite the agreement on the principle of "mazal gorem", medieval rulings split into two polar approaches: the rationalist, lenient approach of Maimonides, who stood almost alone, and the stringent approach of the mainstream of Spanish halakhic decision-making.
The lenient approach: At the head of this approach stands Maimonides, who, in keeping with his rationalist outlook, sought to narrow the scope of the prohibition to the point of abolishing it almost entirely. In his responsa he states that "there is no prohibition in this at all" and regards it as a superstition ("makruh"). In the "Mishneh Torah" he takes a more moderate position and accepts the marriage after the fact, ruling that the couple is not compelled to divorce. His distinctive position stemmed, in all likelihood, from his principled opposition to popular beliefs.
The stringent approach: Opposite him, leading decisors such as the Rosh, the Rashba and the Ritva took a stringent position and held that the third husband must be compelled to divorce his "lethal" wife. The Rosh put it sharply: "de-hamira sakkanta me-issura" ("danger is graver than a prohibition"), and argued that just as the rabbinic court is commanded to keep a person away from transgression, so it is commanded to save him from mortal danger.
Up to Crescas's time, then, the halakhic discussion moved between a rationalist rejection of the prohibition (Maimonides' approach, which the majority rejected) and its stringent acceptance. Crescas, by contrast, would propose a third and original path: acceptance of the basic premise of "mazal gorem", but limitation of its scope by means of philosophical and scientific tools.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Crescas's Central Innovation: Incorporating Astrological Conceptions into Halakhic Rulings
The question of the katlanit became an urgent and practical halakhic issue in the wake of the dramatic historical context of the riots of 5151 (1391). These persecutions left thousands of widows, some of whom had lost their second husband in the riots. The rabbinic leadership was required to respond immediately to this distress, and its response to the crisis reveals different approaches to dealing halakhically with catastrophic events.
To appreciate Crescas's distinctiveness, one must first present the ruling of his colleague, the Rivash (Rabbi Yitzchak bar Sheshet). The Rivash took a lenient approach but based it on terms and concepts drawn from the Talmudic world. He used the concept of "makkat medina" ("a regional calamity"), which is discussed in the laws of damages. Just as in the case of general agricultural damage (such as locusts or drought) the blame is not laid on the private fortune of the tenant, so too in the case of riots or a plague, the husband's death is not to be attributed to the woman's "bad" fortune. This is a legal analogy that limits the scope of astrological responsibility.
Crescas, as emerges from the responsum of his disciple Rabbi Yosef Albo, arrived at the same lenient conclusion, but on an entirely different conceptual basis. Whereas the Rivash operated from within the conceptual world of the Talmud and based his ruling on a legal analogy from the laws of damages, Crescas turned outward and consciously imported terminology and principles from the astrological science of his day in order to ground the same lenient decision. He did not turn to a legal analogy but borrowed the terms and principles directly from the field of astrological science. In his responsum, Albo presents his teacher's central distinction:
It seems to me that this woman is permitted to marry, for although we say that if she married a first husband and he died, and a second and he died, she should not marry a third, not every death is meant, but only the death that comes from the particular judgment; but the death that comes from the general judgment, by plague or by war — no.
Crescas's distinction between "particular judgment" (mishpat prati) and "general judgment" (mishpat kelali) is not a poetic distinction but a precise use of technical terminology from medieval astrological science. The term "mishpat" ("judgment") was used in the Hebrew of that period to describe the laws of astrological influence. The distinction refers to two main branches of astrology:
"Particular judgment" (the astrology of "nativities"): a branch dealing with the fate of an individual person, as determined by the map of the stars at the moment of his birth (horoscope).
"General judgment" (universal astrology): a branch dealing with mass events that affect large groups, peoples and states, such as wars, plagues and natural disasters.
This distinction originates in the writings of the Greek astronomer and astrologer Ptolemy, in his book "Tetrabiblos", and it was widespread among medieval Jewish thinkers, such as Abraham ibn Ezra in his "Sefer ha-Moladot" ("Book of Nativities"). Crescas does not merely adopt the terminology but applies a basic astrological rule: the general judgment prevails over the particular judgment and cancels it. When a person's private fate clashes with a general decree, the general decree is decisive. Therefore, when the husband is killed in war or in a plague, his death is not the result of his wife's "fortune" (the particular judgment), but of the general decree that fell upon the public as a whole. Consequently, there is no reason whatsoever to fear that she poses a danger to a third husband.
But Crescas did not stop there. He incorporated a further principle, one central to his thought, in order to narrow the scope of the prohibition even more and to stress the limits of astrological influence.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. A Complementary Philosophical Thesis: Free Choice versus Astrological Determinism
Crescas's innovation did not end with the distinction between types of astrological decrees. He went on to address the fundamental question of the limits of astrological influence itself, thereby linking his halakhic ruling directly to the basic principles of his philosophical teaching.
In his responsum, Albo cites a further exception that Crescas established to the prohibition of the katlanit: a case in which the husband died "a private death for the sanctification of the Name" (Kiddush Hashem). That is, a situation in which an individual faces the choice between conversion and giving up his life, and chooses death.
And my teacher, Rabbi Even Hasdai, of blessed memory, would further say: it need not be said that one who was killed at the time of the decree, which is a death decreed upon the community, his wife is permitted to marry a third; but even one who was killed by a private death for the sanctification of God's Name, she is permitted to marry a third. And he inferred it from our saying "he fell from a palm tree and died", and they did not say "he went up to the roof and threw himself down and died", for one who dies by choice is included neither in "fortune causes" nor in "the source causes", for choice lies in man's hand, and this is the root of our Torah...
The central argument here is revolutionary in its halakhic context: an act performed out of absolute free choice, such as giving up one's life for the sanctification of the Name, is not subject to astrological decrees. Astrological fate ("mazal gorem") governs only events that do not depend on human choice, such as accidents or illnesses. Free choice, by contrast, breaks through the bounds of stellar determinism.
This idea was not new to the philosophical tradition. Thinkers such as Maimonides and Gersonides (Ralbag) had already established that the influence of the stars does not govern man's voluntary acts. Crescas's innovation, however, lies in applying this philosophical principle as an interpretive and halakhic tool within a specific question. Although there is a hypothesis in the scholarship that the detailed philosophical reasoning is Albo's addition, the direct connection of the argument to principles that Crescas himself formulated in "Or Hashem" ties the ruling and its reasoning to the teacher, not to the disciple. He thereby links his ruling directly to his philosophical thought as expressed in his book "Or Hashem". There, in the discussion of the influence of the heavenly bodies, he states:
"For although they [the heavenly bodies] act upon and prepare matter, they do not act by necessity; and all the more so in man, who is possessed of intellect and choice."
His ruling on the katlanit is nothing other than a halakhic application of this philosophical principle. To show that this is not an exceptional phenomenon but a systematic pattern, further examples of the integration of philosophy and science into the halakhic writing of Crescas and his circle must be examined.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The Intellectual Circle: A Pattern of Integration between Philosophy and Halakha
The incorporation of astrological and philosophical conceptions in the question of the katlanit was not an isolated case but a systematic feature of the intellectual approach of Crescas and of some of his disciples and colleagues. Despite the scarcity of halakhic sources that have survived from this circle, the extant remnants point to a consistent tendency to use tools from the fields of logic, science and philosophy to analyze halakhic questions.
4.1. Logical Techniques in Crescas's Passover Sermon
In the halakhic part of the Passover sermon, Crescas does not engage in ordinary Talmudic pilpul but in constructing a taxonomy (a systematic classification) of the commandments of the festival. He does so by means of two techniques drawn from philosophical logic:
Dichotomous divisions: Crescas classifies the commandments of the festival in a series of binary divisions: between commandments common to the festivals and commandments unique to Passover; between commandments dependent on the Temple and commandments that apply at all times; between positive commandments and prohibitions. This structure recalls the "Porphyrian tree" (arbor porphyriana) of the classical logical tradition – a technique that organizes concepts from the general to the particular through a series of binary divisions – and is not common in the halakhic literature that preceded him.
Breaking down definitions: After the initial classification, Crescas focuses on the commandment of removing leaven (bi'ur chametz), defines it, and then breaks the definition down into its basic components. He shows how each component of the definition is essential and establishes a separate halakhic principle. This is a distinctly philosophical technique, which he also used in his book "Or Hashem" to analyze concepts such as prophecy, and it scarcely appears in halakhic literature before him.
4.2. The Use of the Sciences in the Responsum of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Shmuel ben Shealtiel
Crescas's colleague, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Shmuel ben Shealtiel, was asked a technical halakhic question: whether it is permitted to sew a Torah scroll with strings made of gut that are used for musical instruments. In order to define precisely the Talmudic term "gidin" ("sinews", from which the threads must be made), he did not content himself with rabbinic sources but quoted a passage from a Hebrew translation of the book of the Muslim philosopher and physician Avicenna (Ibn Sina), "The Canon of Medicine". Rabbi Yitzchak was well aware of the novelty of this step, and added words of apology that attest to it:
"Perhaps you will laugh at me for bringing the words of Ibn Sina in support, and say: we do [not] learn words of Torah from idle words."
This apology reveals both the sensitivity to the novelty of introducing a scientific-philosophical source into a halakhic discussion and the determination to do so when it is needed to clarify the question.
4.3. Scholastic Methodology in the Sermon of Rabbi Zerahiah ha-Levi Saladin
Rabbi Zerahiah ha-Levi Saladin, Crescas's disciple and his successor in the leadership of the communities of Aragon, illustrates the profound influence of philosophical methodology on this circle. In a sermon on whether vows are advisable, he builds the discussion in the format of a scholastic question (quaestio disputata), which was customary in the Christian universities of his day. The structure includes:
Presentation of a question (quaestio).
Arguments for the two opposing sides.
Decision and verdict (determinatio).
Moreover, the influence is not merely formal. An analysis of the sermon's content reveals that Rabbi Zerahiah's arguments, and even his formulations, draw directly on the discussion by the Christian philosopher Thomas Aquinas of precisely the same subject in his "Summa Theologiae". This attests to a broad intellectual openness and to a willingness to draw not only tools but also contents from the surrounding philosophical world.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Summary and Conclusions
This article has examined the influences of philosophy and science on the halakhic writing of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas and his circle. The analysis of his ruling on the question of the "lethal woman" revealed an innovative approach, which combines principles from astrology and from philosophy in order to arrive at a lenient halakhic decision. Further examples from his circle – the use of Aristotelian logic in Crescas's Passover sermon, the quotation from the writings of Ibn Sina in the responsum of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Shealtiel, and the adoption of scholastic methodology and content in the sermon of Rabbi Zerahiah ha-Levi Saladin – support the claim that this is not an isolated case but a consistent intellectual pattern.
The significance of the findings is far-reaching. Although only a few remnants of his halakhic writing have survived, almost all of them attest to a consistent willingness to incorporate philosophical and scientific concepts, tools and ideas into halakhic discussions. This approach challenges the accepted description of Crescas as an "anti-rationalist". True, in his book "Or Hashem" he sharply attacked the positions of Aristotle and Maimonides, but this critique stemmed not from a rejection of philosophy as a tool but from a deep commitment to its critical and correct use.
Crescas's halakhic enterprise, therefore, is not an appendix to his philosophical enterprise but the laboratory in which his principles were applied. He was not a critic of rationality but the architect of a new halakhic rationality – one that is not afraid to draw on every source of knowledge in order to deepen its understanding and establish its authority.
The Centrality of Love in the Theology of Hasdai Crescas
Introduction: Defining the Thesis and Outlining the Argument
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (c. 1340-1410) stands as one of the central and revolutionary thinkers of medieval Jewish thought. His activity took place in a period of deep theological and social crisis in Spanish Jewry, a period marked by growing tension in the face of militant Christianity and by internal criticism of the path of philosophical rationalism. Within this turbulent reality, Crescas formulated an original and powerful theological doctrine, which offers a new way of understanding the relations between God, man and the world.
The central thesis of this article is that Crescas's doctrine of love is not merely a side topic in his thought but constitutes the founding and unifying principle of his mature theological system. This view echoes the conclusions of pioneering scholars such as Ephraim Elimelech Urbach, who defined love as "the key to his entire system", but it seeks to establish it not only as a general conclusion but as a finding that emerges from a developmental textual analysis. Contrary to interpretations that see it as just one more philosophical theme, it is argued here that love is the "middle bar" (the linchpin) of his late system, the "foundation of foundations" that gives coherence and meaning to the whole of his thought – from his conception of God and creation to the purpose of the commandments and providence.
To truly grasp the depth of Crescas's revolution, we must first become textual archaeologists. His masterpiece, "Or Hashem", is not a monolithic text but a multi-layered work that reveals a profound intellectual journey. The article will trace the construction of this thesis in three stages. First, the developmental process of his thought will be analyzed in order to establish the "doctrine of love" as the latest and most fully formed layer of his work. Next, the theological pillars of this doctrine will be examined: the conception of the loving God, creation as an expression of love, providence as a dialogue of love, and the commandments as the practical path to its realization. Finally, Crescas's thought will be placed in its twofold polemical context – as a frontal attack on Jewish rationalism from within, and as a sophisticated theological response to the challenge posed by Christianity from without.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part One: The Crystallization of the "Doctrine of Love" in "Or Hashem"
Understanding the thought of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas requires a methodological approach that recognizes that his book "Or Hashem" is not all of one piece. It is a multifaceted work that was edited over many years and in which different conceptual strata are discernible. Identifying the "stratum of love" as a late and fully formed layer of his thought is not merely a technical matter; it is the key to understanding the coherence and power of his final doctrine. I shall argue that different strata can be identified in the text, but I must stress that, however solid this claim may be, it cannot go beyond the bounds of conjecture. Only by identifying this mature and final layer – the "doctrine of love" – can the coherence of the whole system be deciphered and its true power understood.

It is the hermeneutical key to his work. It resolves apparent contradictions and reveals that his final theological vision is an integrative system unified by a single powerful principle: love. Having established the doctrine of love as the most fully formed and highest layer of his thought, we can now examine its theological foundations.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part Two: The Theological Pillars of the Doctrine of Love
Having established the doctrine of love as the late and fully formed layer of Crescas's thought, this part will analyze its theological foundations. We shall see how the supremacy of the idea of love is expressed not only on the emotional plane but brings about a veritable revolution in the basic conceptions of Jewish thought: the conception of God, creation, providence and the purpose of the commandments. Each of these pillars is reshaped in the light of the principle of love, and together they form a complete and coherent theological system.
2.1 The Loving God: A Polemic against the Intellectual-Impersonal Conception
Crescas's first and decisive step in establishing the doctrine of love is to free the conception of God from the shackles of rationalism. He dismantles the Maimonidean framework of the "doctrine of negative attributes" – which denied the ascription of positive qualities to God for fear of impairing His unity – and builds in its place the doctrine of "essential attributes". This doctrine holds that positive attributes (such as knowing, able, willing) may be ascribed to God not as God's very essence but as expressions that flow from His essence without defining it. This move was not merely a philosophical exercise; it was a necessary condition for constructing a theology centred on a personal, active and loving God. It allows Crescas to add revolutionary attributes such as "loving" and **"rejoicing"**, which do not describe being affected (a passive emotional response) but an active deed that flows from His perfection.
The polemical significance of this move is enormous. It is a direct attack on the rationalist conception of God held by Maimonides and Gersonides (Ralbag), which described God as a purely intellectual being, "intellect, intellecting subject and intellected object", that is, an impersonal being whose chief concern is intellectual self-cognition. Crescas's God, by contrast, is a personal and volitional God. He is not a remote being who can be approached only through philosophical contemplation, but a loving God with whom a relationship of dialogue and emotional closeness can be established.
2.2 Creation and Providence as an Expression of God's Love
The conception of the loving God fundamentally changes the understanding of creation and providence. Crescas rejects the traditional philosophical debate over the eternity or creation of the world and proposes in its place a dynamic model of continuous creation. He sees in the blessing "who in His goodness renews every day, continually, the work of creation" not merely a poetic metaphor but a precise description of reality. Creation is an expression of the constant overflow (shefa) of God's love, which flows into the world and sustains it at every single moment. The world is not the product of logical necessity but the fruit of the Creator's good and loving will.
Divine providence is a direct continuation of creation out of love. Crescas distinguishes between two types of providence:
General providence: This is a deterministic-astral providence, which applies to nature and to the nations of the world through the system of the stars and constellations. It expresses the general order that God established out of His will to do good to the whole of creation.
Special providence: This is a providence that goes beyond the astral order and applies to the people of Israel. It does not stem from the laws of nature but from a relationship of mutual love. Man's love for God is not merely a passive response; it is an active force that **"breaks through"** the general cosmic determinism. This love arouses God's special and direct providence, and thereby changes the cosmic order for Israel.
2.3 The Human Response: The Commandments as the Path of Love
If God, creation and special providence are founded on love, what, then, is the supreme purpose of the human response expressed in the Torah? Crescas's answer poses a further challenge to rationalism. Whereas the philosophers saw the commandments as a means of perfecting the intellect, Crescas sees their aim as the purification and refinement of the soul so as to enable it to love God. The commandments are a constant training in overcoming "the inclination to materiality", and they thereby prepare a person for the supreme religious act – the love of God.
Love is not one-directional; it is a dynamic, interactive cycle between man and God:
Man's love for God: expressed in the fulfilment of the commandments with an intention of devotion (devekut) and love, and not out of a quest for reward or intellectual perfection. Abraham's love, expressed in his readiness to offer the sacrifice of the Binding (the Akedah), is the archetype of this love.
The arousal of God's love: the human act of love "draws" and arouses God's special love towards the loving person or people. This love breaks through the laws of nature and establishes a direct and personal providence.
Providence of love: God's special love is expressed in the giving of the Torah and the commandments, which are themselves the instrument that enables man to deepen his love, and so the cycle begins again.
Now that the theological foundations of the doctrine of love have been clarified, it can be placed, in its full force, within the twofold polemical context of its time.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part Three: The Polemical Context: War on Two Fronts
Hasdai Crescas's doctrine of love did not grow in a vacuum. It constitutes a complex and sophisticated theological response to the two central challenges that faced Spanish Jewry in his generation: from within, the challenge of philosophical rationalism, which threatened to empty Judaism of its emotional content; and from without, the growing pressure of Christian theology, which placed love at its centre and attacked Judaism as a religion of dry law. Crescas's doctrine is thus a struggle on two fronts, offering an authentic and vital Jewish alternative to both threats at once.
3.1 The Internal Front: Challenging Jewish Rationalism
Crescas's critique of Jewish rationalism does not amount to a dispute over this or that philosophical detail; it is an attack on the entire religious worldview. The central contrasts can be summarized as follows:
The human ideal: Whereas the rationalists set up the **"philosopher"** – the person who has attained intellectual perfection – as the supreme ideal, Crescas sets against him the **"hasid"** (the pious one). These are not merely two different ideals but two fundamental conceptions of the bond between man and God: one based on intellectual contemplation of an impersonal principle, the other on an emotional and volitional bond with a personal God.
The essence of religion: For the rationalists, religion is a path to the intellectual apprehension of philosophical truths. For Crescas, the essence of religion is a relationship of love between man and God. The commandments are not a means of perfecting knowledge but the practical way to purify the soul and make this bond of love possible.
The nature of God: The rationalist God is an impersonal God, "pure intellect". Crescas, by contrast, presents a personal, loving and volitional God, who chooses Israel out of love and watches over them with special providence.
3.2 The External Front: Dialogue with Christian Thought
Crescas's strategy towards Christianity is particularly sophisticated. Instead of rejecting Christian theological concepts out of hand, he adopts them, "converts" them, and gives them a new and original meaning within a Jewish-halakhic framework. He thereby creates a strong Jewish alternative, which uses the opponent's own weapon in order to defeat him.
Original sin: Crescas accepts the idea of original sin, but redefines it not as a theological sin requiring mystical redemption but as an **"inclination to materiality"** and a lust inherent in human nature. Redemption from it comes not through faith in Jesus but through the covenant of circumcision and the Torah, which refine the body and make the love of God possible.
Sacrifice: Against the idea of the atoning sacrifice of Jesus on the cross, Crescas sets the Binding of Isaac (the Akedah) as the archetype of the "sacrifice of love". Abraham's readiness to sacrifice his son out of absolute love for God is the founding act, which established God's special relationship to the people of Israel and His special providence over them.
New covenant: Crescas takes the Christian concept of the "new covenant" and argues that the covenant of circumcision is itself the true "new covenant". It is this covenant that renewed the bond between man and God after original sin, and it is this covenant that symbolizes the election of the people of Israel.
This sophisticated polemical strategy enabled Crescas to deal simultaneously with the internal and the external challenge, and to offer a warm, emotion-filled Jewish alternative to rationalism, while showing how the core concepts of Christianity find their complete and true expression precisely within halakhic Judaism.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion: Hasdai Crescas as a Theological Revolutionary
At the end of this course of argument, the central claim of the article is established and clarified: Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's doctrine of love is not merely a theme in his thought but the foundation of foundations of his mature theological system. It is the organizing principle that gives meaning, depth and coherence to the whole of his thought, and turns him from a thinker who reacts to crises into a thinker who creates a new paradigm. The analysis of the development of his thought shows how love became, in the late stage of his work, the key by means of which he reshaped the conception of God, creation, providence and the purpose of religious existence.
We have seen how this doctrine constituted a twofold and sophisticated response to the challenges of his generation. From within, it offered a warm and personal spiritual alternative to what was perceived as the intellectual coldness of rationalist philosophy. From without, it presented an authentic and powerful Jewish answer to the theological challenge posed by Christianity, by "converting" key Christian concepts and pointing to their true realization in Judaism.
In light of this, Crescas should be seen not only as a brilliant philosopher but as a theological revolutionary. In response to the crises of his generation, he did not content himself with minor corrections but placed love at the centre of religious existence. In "converting" Christian concepts, he did not seek to draw closer to Christianity, but sought "to restore the crown to its former glory" and, in essence, "to return to the faith of biblical Judaism" – to the faith of "And you shall love the Lord your God" and to God's love for Israel, in the spirit of "I have loved you with an everlasting love". He thereby offered a new and influential path in Jewish thought, a path that emphasizes the living, emotional and interactive dialogue between man and his God.
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas: A Survey of Academic Research on His Thought and Writings
The continuing academic engagement with the thought of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas, as reflected in the publications of the Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities, attests to his standing as one of the central thinkers of medieval Jewish philosophy. His teaching, including his principal work "Or Hashem", continues to be fertile ground for research. This document will survey and analyze the contribution of selected publications of the Academy to the understanding of his philosophical teaching, relying exclusively on the information that appears in the Academy's catalogue of publications. Through this focused examination, we shall sketch the outlines of his intellectual figure as it is reflected in the mirror of contemporary research.
1. The Rediscovery of a Hidden Work: The "Passover Sermon" according to the Research of Aviezer Ravitzky
One of the central challenges in the study of medieval Jewish thought lies in locating, deciphering and editing manuscripts that were forgotten over the generations or whose authorship was cast in doubt. The discovery of hidden texts can shed new light on entire periods, clarify intricate philosophical questions and reveal unfamiliar facets of the teaching of central thinkers. Prof. Aviezer Ravitzky's research on Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's "Passover Sermon", as described in his book "Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's Passover Sermon and Studies in His Philosophical Teaching", clearly exemplifies this research process and underlines its importance for understanding Crescas's spiritual world.
1.1. The Character of the "Passover Sermon" and Its Importance
The "Passover Sermon" is a short philosophical work that lay hidden in manuscripts and whose identity was forgotten over time, to the point that scholars' attention was diverted from it. According to the description of Ravitzky's book, the importance of the work stems from its contribution to the understanding of various and diverse aspects of Crescas's thought and activity.
The work's main contributions, as emerges from the research, are:
Clarifying fundamental questions: The work clarifies basic philosophical and historical questions in the study of Crescas's teaching, and thereby serves as an important interpretive tool for understanding his world of ideas.
Information on his halakhic approach: Beyond the philosophical discussion, the sermon provides information concerning Crescas's halakhic approach, and allows a glimpse into a further, less-studied aspect of his personality.
Verification of authorship: The first part of Ravitzky's study is devoted to proving that Rabbi Hasdai Crescas is indeed the author of the sermon, thereby giving the text scholarly validity and restoring it to the corpus attributed to the thinker.
1.2. Comparative Analysis with the Book "Or Hashem"
The research methodology that Ravitzky adopts, as described in the catalogue, is based on comparative analysis. He discusses fundamental questions in Crescas's philosophical teaching through a systematic comparison between the short, dedicated text of the "Passover Sermon" and his comprehensive work, "Or Hashem". This approach makes it possible to examine how ideas presented concisely in the sermon are developed and expanded in his principal work, and conversely – how the sermon clarifies and distils complex concepts from "Or Hashem".
This discussion, which focuses on a specific work, serves as a starting point for a broader examination of the intellectual contexts in which Crescas worked and which shaped his thought.

Rabbi Hasdai Crescas: A Groundbreaking Integration of Philosophy and Halakha in Medieval Spain
1. Introduction: The Complex Figure of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (Rahak) stands as one of the most central, complex and influential figures in Jewish thought of the late Middle Ages. His multifaceted intellectual legacy confronts us with a constant tension: on the one hand, he is known as a profound and innovative philosopher, the author of "Or Hashem" and a sharp critic of the Aristotelian rationalism that characterized the thought of Maimonides and Gersonides. On the other hand, his contemporaries recognized him as one of the greatest Torah scholars in Spain, an esteemed halakhic decisor and a communal leader who aspired to bring about a revolution in the field of halakhic codification. His image as a critic of philosophy has more than once overshadowed his contribution as a halakhist, creating a partial picture of his thought.
The aim of this article is to examine Crescas's twofold legacy, focusing on the unique points of contact between his philosophical world and his halakhic world. It will be argued that an in-depth analysis of his rulings and of the remnants of his halakhic writings reveals a picture utterly different from the accepted one. It turns out that Crescas not only did not refrain from using philosophical tools, but systematically and consistently incorporated concepts, terminology and methods of thinking from the world of philosophy, logic and science into the heart of halakhic discussion. Uncovering this facet of his legacy challenges his accepted labelling as an "anti-rationalist" and presents him as an integrative thinker, who saw in the external sciences powerful tools for understanding the Torah and deciding its law. An examination of the intellectual background from which he emerged will help us understand the depth of the innovation in his approach.
2. The Formative Years and the Intellectual Foundations
To appreciate correctly the innovation of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas, it is essential to understand the educational frameworks and the central figures that shaped his intellectual path. The background from which he emerged provides the key to understanding his rare ability to combine the worlds of halakha and philosophy in so original a way.
Crescas began his studies, in all likelihood, with his grandfather, Rabbi Hasdai Crescas the Elder, who himself wrote halakhic rulings. However, he acquired his deep and comprehensive education in the study house of his principal teacher, Rabbi Nissim Gerondi (the Ran), in Barcelona. The Ran's study house was a fertile ground in which in-depth halakhic study merged with extensive engagement in philosophical thought. In this intellectual environment Crescas became one of the Ran's outstanding disciples, both in halakha and in philosophy, and absorbed the ability to move freely between the two fields.
Later on, Crescas established his standing as a spiritual and halakhic leader in his own right. He founded study houses in Barcelona and Saragossa and raised many disciples, who continued his path. Among his disciples was Rabbi Yosef Chaviva, who would become one of the important Talmud commentators in Spain in the 15th century. The consolidation of his standing as a senior decisor, whom various sages used to consult on intricate halakhic questions, fed his literary ambition to compose a comprehensive halakhic work that would reflect his distinctive approach.
3. The Decisor and Legislator: A Lost Halakhic Legacy and Revealing Remnants
Every attempt to reconstruct the halakhic world of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas encounters a significant research challenge. Unfortunately, the overwhelming majority of his halakhic writings were lost over the generations, leaving a great void in our understanding of his enterprise in this field. Not a single book of his principal works has survived – not a book of rulings, not a commentary on the Talmud, and not even an orderly collection of his responsa. This fact is particularly regrettable in light of his own testimony to his aspiration to compose a comprehensive halakhic code that would replace Maimonides' "Mishneh Torah" and offer an alternative approach to codification.
Despite this loss, the few remnants that remain in our hands provide a rare and valuable glimpse into his distinctive methodology. His innovative halakhic approach can be discerned by analyzing three fragmentary sources:
The critique of Maimonides' codification: a short passage that appears in the introduction to his philosophical book "Or Hashem", in which he outlines his alternative approach to the arrangement of halakha.
A discussion of the laws of Passover: a halakhic passage found in the "Passover Sermon", the only sermon of Crescas to have survived in its entirety.
A ruling on the "lethal woman": a revolutionary ruling documented in a halakhic responsum written by his disciple, Rabbi Yosef Albo, in the name of his teacher.
These sources, and especially Albo's responsum, are a key to understanding the original combination of philosophy, science and halakhic decision-making in his teaching – a combination that attests to a broad intellectual horizon and to a willingness to adopt tools from external fields for the purpose of deciding the law.
4. The Case of the "Lethal Woman": A Synthesis of Halakha, Astrology and Free Choice
The question of the "lethal woman" is a central test case, which powerfully reveals the depth of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's intellectual innovation. His handling of this intricate halakhic question, which arose in the wake of an acute historical crisis, is not merely an example of a ruling sensitive to human distress but a brilliant intellectual move. In his ruling, Crescas demonstrates how an ancient halakhic tradition can be combined with the scientific and philosophical worldviews of his time in order to arrive at a groundbreaking decision.
4.1 The Historical and Halakhic Background
The halakhic question arose in all its acuteness after the riots of 5151 (1391), a traumatic event in which thousands of Jews were killed throughout Spain. In the wake of the riots, the communities had to deal with a difficult halakhic and social problem: a large number of widows whose second husbands had been killed in the riots. According to Talmudic law, a woman whose two husbands have died is called a "katlanit" ("lethal woman"), and she is forbidden to marry a third time for fear that she will endanger her next husband as well.
The Talmudic discussion of the cause of the husbands' death revolves around a dispute among the Amoraim:
"The source causes" (ma'ayan gorem): a view that sees the cause as biological-medical (for example, a contagious venereal disease).
"Fortune causes" (mazal gorem): a view that sees the cause as the woman's bad astrological fate.
The overwhelming majority of the medieval sages adopted the approach of "mazal gorem" as the main explanation. An exceptional position was that of Maimonides, who, out of his rationalist outlook, saw the prohibition as a superstition and tended to be considerably lenient about it. However, Maimonides' lenient ruling was rejected by most of the decisors, who held a more stringent approach.
4.2 Crescas's Innovative Ruling and Its Reasons
Against this background, Crescas's ruling, which has reached us exclusively through the responsum of his disciple Rabbi Yosef Albo, was revolutionary. Crescas ruled unequivocally that a woman whose husband was killed in a mass event such as a plague, a war or riots is not considered a "katlanit" and is permitted to marry. To appreciate the full extent of his innovation, his approach must be compared with that of his colleague, the Rivash (Rabbi Yitzchak bar Sheshet). The Rivash, too, reached a similar halakhic conclusion and permitted the widows to marry, but his reasons were all drawn from within the traditional world of halakha. He based his ruling on a Talmudic analogy to the law of "makkat medina" ("a regional calamity") – a general disaster on account of which the damage is not attributed to a person's private fortune. Whereas the Rivash remained faithful to the accepted interpretive tools, Crescas consciously chose to abandon them. In order to decide this distinctly Talmudic question, Crescas borrowed the conceptual basis for his ruling not from the world of images of the Talmud but directly from the scientific terminology of the astrology of his day.
Crescas based his ruling on the distinction between "particular judgment" and **"general judgment"**:
"General judgment": a technical term taken from the field of universal astrology, which examines the influence of the heavenly bodies on mass events that affect large groups (such as wars and plagues).
"Particular judgment": a term referring to the astrology of nativities (natal astrology), which deals with the fate of an individual person on the basis of his horoscope.
The central scientific principle that Crescas used, as formulated by thinkers such as Ptolemy and Ibn Ezra, holds that the general prevails over the particular. That is, when a clash occurs between a general astrological decree and a particular one, the general decree is decisive. Therefore, when the husband dies in a general event such as riots, his death is not attributed to the woman's private "fortune" but to the "general judgment" that fell upon the community as a whole.
In addition, Crescas proposed a second exception, no less important, based on a philosophical principle: a case in which the husband chose to die for the sanctification of the Name as an individual. His reasoning was that man's free choice prevails over the astrological decree. Crescas himself established this principle in his book "Or Hashem", where he argued that the influence of the stars does not act by necessity on a person "possessed of intellect and choice". A death that results from a conscious choice is not like an accidental death ("he fell from a palm tree and died"), and therefore cannot be attributed to fortune.
This ruling is not merely a halakhic solution to social distress. It is a brilliant intellectual move, which applies philosophical and scientific principles to the deciding of a halakhic case and attests to a broad and integrative pattern of thinking that characterized Crescas's circle.
5. The Philosophical Method as a Halakhic Tool: Further Examples from Crescas's Circle
The sophisticated use of astrological and philosophical concepts in the ruling on the "lethal woman" was not the flash of inspiration of a lone thinker, but the expression of a systematic methodology that characterized an entire intellectual circle that formed around Crescas. This circle displayed a deep openness and a willingness to incorporate modes of thinking, terminology and concepts from the worlds of philosophy, logic and science into halakhic discussion. The following examples, drawn from the writings of Crescas, his colleagues and his disciples, illustrate the depth and scope of this approach.
5.1 Logical Taxonomy in the "Passover Sermon"
In the halakhic part of the "Passover Sermon", his only surviving sermon, Crescas demonstrates a distinct use of a classical logical-philosophical tool. In order to classify the commandments of the festival, he builds an orderly taxonomy based on a series of dichotomous (binary) divisions descending from the general to the particular. He begins with the division between commandments common to the festivals and commandments unique to Passover, continues with the division between commandments dependent on the Temple and commandments that apply at all times, and so on. This technique, known as the "Porphyrian tree" (arbor porphyriana), is a distinctly logical tool that medieval thinkers used to define concepts. Its use in the context of halakhic classification was, in all likelihood, an innovation of Crescas, attesting to his desire to bring order and conceptual clarity into the world of halakha.
5.2 Scientific Authority in Halakhic Decision-Making
Another fascinating example comes from the responsum of Crescas's colleague, Rabbi Yitzchak ben Shmuel ben Shealtiel. When he was asked whether it is permitted to sew a Torah scroll with sinews used in making musical instruments, he had to define an anatomical term precisely. To do so, he does not content himself with rabbinic sources but quotes directly from the book "The Canon of Medicine" by the renowned Muslim philosopher and physician Ibn Sina. Rabbi Yitzchak is well aware of the novelty of this step, and even anticipates possible criticism, writing: "Perhaps you will laugh at me for bringing the words of Ibn Sina in support, and say: we do not learn words of Torah from idle words." Nevertheless, he chooses to rely on an external scientific authority, out of an understanding that scientific precision is essential to the halakhic decision.
5.3 Scholastic Methodology in Sermons
The deepest philosophical influence can be found in the sermon of Crescas's disciple and successor, Rabbi Zerahiah ha-Levi Saladin, which discusses whether it is advisable to take vows. The entire sermon is built in the format of a scholastic "disputed question" (quaestio disputata) – a structure of discussion that was widespread in the Christian universities of the Middle Ages. Rabbi Zerahiah opens by presenting a question, brings a series of arguments in favour of vows and a series of arguments against them, and finally decides the issue. He even uses technical terms such as "derush be-mahloket" ("a disputed inquiry") and "pesak din ha-derush" ("the verdict of the inquiry"), which are a direct translation of scholastic terminology. Research has even revealed that Rabbi Zerahiah borrowed not only the structure of the discussion but also many of the arguments themselves directly from the writings of the Christian philosopher Thomas Aquinas.
These examples paint a clear picture of a lively, open and daring intellectual circle, led by Crescas, which was not afraid to blur the accepted boundaries between Torah and wisdom.
6. Conclusion: A Reassessment of the Legacy of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas
The few remnants that remain of the halakhic writings of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas and his circle reveal a rich and surprising intellectual picture. As we have seen, the analysis of his rulings, his sermons and the writings of his disciples attests to a consistent and systematic willingness to incorporate concepts, terminology and modes of thinking from the world of philosophy, logic and science into the very heart of halakhic discussion. From the use of astrological terminology to permit a "lethal woman" to marry, through the application of a logical taxonomy to the classification of commandments, to the adoption of scholastic structures for halakhic discussion – in all of these there emerges a thinker who saw in external fields of knowledge a legitimate and useful source for understanding the Torah and deciding its law.
These findings call for a reassessment of the label "anti-rationalist" that has been attached to Crescas. Despite his trenchant critique of specific philosophical conclusions of Aristotle, Maimonides and Gersonides, he was far from being a sweeping opponent of the use of philosophical tools. On the contrary: his halakhic activity proves that he regarded philosophy and science as important and valued tools, capable of lending precision, order and depth to halakhic thinking. His critique was directed not against reason itself, but against what he saw as its dogmatic and uncritical use.
The true legacy of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas, then, is that of an integrative and groundbreaking thinker. He not only offered a philosophical alternative to the Aristotelian tradition, but also creatively blurred the accepted boundaries between the world of halakha and the world of wisdom. He thereby set up a daring model of halakhic decision-making that does not shut itself up in its own world, but draws consciously and critically on the best of human wisdom, leaving a legacy of integrative thought that challenges the boundaries of Jewish discourse to this day.
The Conceptual and Textual Development of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's "Or Hashem": An Analysis of the Archaeological Layers of the Text
Opening: "Or Hashem" as a Multifaceted Work
For generations, the accepted view in the study of Jewish thought identified the concept of "love" as the very heart of the philosophical thought of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (Rahak). Prominent scholars, such as S. B. Urbach, determined that "love is the key to Crescas's entire system", and Eliezer Schweid added that "the foundation of foundations in Crescas's teaching is the doctrine of love". However, despite the agreed conceptual centrality of this concept, the structure of the book "Or Hashem" does not reflect this coherence. The idea of love appears in isolated passages, at times as a late addition to existing discussions, and not as a central axis that organizes the work as a whole. This gap between content and structure indicates that "Or Hashem" is not a monolithic work but a multi-layered text that developed over time.
This monograph adopts and develops the founding thesis presented by Eilon Shamir in his master's thesis, according to which the book "Or Hashem" is not a monolithic work but a text that took shape in stages, and the "doctrine of love" represents the latest, most mature and most comprehensive stratum of Crescas's thought. It is not the starting point of his thought but its intellectual peak. We shall establish and expand his philological findings, deepen the theological analysis, and place the development of Crescas's thought in a sharpened polemical context.
To establish this claim, the document will be divided into three main parts. In the first part, we shall establish philologically the identification of the "stratum of love" as a late and distinct editorial layer within the text. In the second part, we shall delve into the rich theology of this stratum and analyze how the concept of love becomes a cosmic principle that constitutes God's relation to the world, creation, providence and the purpose of man. In the third part, we shall place the development of the doctrine of love in its historical context and show how it functions as a twofold and sophisticated polemic: both against Jewish philosophical rationalism and against Christian theology.
First, we must establish the textual claim regarding the existence of different strata in the book. This philological grounding is a necessary foundation for the in-depth conceptual analysis that will follow it, and will enable us to understand Crescas's spiritual journey from a rigid philosophical determinism to a worldview at whose centre stands love.
Part One: The Stratigraphy of "Or Hashem": Establishing the "Stratum of Love" as a Late Editorial Layer
Understanding the development of Crescas's thought requires an archaeological approach to the text of "Or Hashem". The book as it lies before us does not reflect a uniform line of thought but is evidence of a lengthy process of writing, editing and additions. The analysis of the editorial layers is not merely a technical matter; it is the key to uncovering the conceptual tensions, the changes and the developments that took place in Crescas's thought over his turbulent years of creativity. The analysis below will propose a persuasive developmental model, based on textual and conceptual evidence. Although this model should be regarded as a learned conjecture rather than a proven fact, it provides the most powerful key at our disposal for deciphering the development of Crescas's thought. The methodology we shall use to identify the different strata will include four main tools: analysis of conceptual differences and shifts in theological emphasis, examination of the closing formulas that seal discussions, systematic comparison with the "Passover Sermon", and analysis of semantic fields and changes in terminology.
A.1. Textual Evidence from the Treatise "On Choice" (Treatise II, Principle 5)
Principle 5 of the second treatise, which deals with the question of free choice, is perhaps the clearest example of the multi-layered structure of "Or Hashem". A close analysis of the principle reveals at least three stages in the development of Crescas's thought.
The first layer: the "Abnerian stratum" (chapters 1–4)
The first four chapters of the principle present a sharply deterministic conception, deeply influenced by the thought of the apostate Abner of Burgos. The central idea, summed up in the formula "possible in respect of itself, and necessary in respect of its causes", holds that although a human action has the potential to be otherwise, in practice it is always determined necessarily by the chain of causes that precede it. This stratum focuses on the intellectual and doxastic aspect of the consciousness of freedom. Unusually, the fourth chapter is sealed with the closing formula typical of the book's principles ("and praise be to God alone, who is exalted above all blessing and praise"), which indicates that in an early edition of the work the discussion of the question of choice ended here.
The second layer: the "stratum of the sermon" (chapters 5–6)
After the closing formula, the discussion opens anew in chapters 5–6, with a dramatic change of emphasis. Here, concepts such as "will", "joy" and **"arevut"** (delight/pleasure) take centre stage. Crescas argues that the intellectual and doxastic plane is indeed subject to determinism, but man's true space of choice lies on the volitional-emotional plane. Man is free to choose whether to rejoice in his faith, whether to feel "arevut" in the fulfilment of the commandments. This stratum parallels almost completely extensive passages of Crescas's "Passover Sermon", a work that in all likelihood preceded the final version of "Or Hashem". The comparison between the texts reveals an almost complete identity, but also a decisive difference: the complete absence of the concept of "love".
