The third layer: the "stratum of love" (the textual "seam")
Within the discussion of the "stratum of the sermon", on page 221 (according to the page numbering of the Fisher edition, Jerusalem 5750), we find a short passage that bears witness to a late attempt by Crescas to incorporate his mature conception of love into the early text. In this passage, the word "love" appears for the first time in this context: "And this is because He, may He be blessed, is in the utmost of love and delight (arevut) to bestow and to do good...". The sudden appearance of the word "love" alongside "arevut", and the attempt to blur the boundaries between them, reveal a textual "seam". This is a moment at which Crescas tries to widen the discussion of "arevut" and "joy" so that it also includes the more comprehensive concept of "love".
A.2. Textual Evidence from the Treatise "On Providence" (Treatise II, Principle 2)
A similar structure of editorial layers can also be identified in the principle dealing with divine providence. Here too, the text reflects a clear conceptual development from an early stage to a late one.
The early stratum: "providence as knowledge"
The first three chapters of the principle are devoted to a trenchant polemic against the view of Gersonides, who argued that God does not know the changing particulars of the world. Crescas, in the spirit of the thought of Abner of Burgos, argues forcefully that God knows every single particular, and that His providence is an expression of His absolute knowledge. The emphasis in this stratum is cognitive: providence is a function of God's knowledge.
The late stratum: "providence as love"
At the end of chapter 4 and in chapter 5, a dramatic change of emphasis occurs. A new dimension is added to the discussion of God's knowledge: providence is not merely knowledge but an expression of God's love, realized through a constant "bestowal" of good upon the world. The transition from "providence as knowledge" to "providence as love" is not merely a shift of emphasis but a late conceptual addition that gives a new and deeper interpretation to the whole discussion. Love becomes the cause and the essence of providence.
A.3. Synthesis and Conclusions: A Chronological Reconstruction of the Development of "Or Hashem"
The textual evidence presented enables us to reconstruct the process of the development of "Or Hashem" and to identify three main stages in Crescas's thought:
Stage A (the "Abnerian" stratum): an early stage characterized by a rigid determinism, based on a conception of providence as God's absolute knowledge of all particulars. This stage reflects the profound influence of Abner of Burgos and the initial polemic with Jewish rationalism.
Stage B (the stratum of the "Passover Sermon"): the development of an anti-intellectualist approach, responding to the rigid determinism. At this stage, human freedom lies not on the intellectual plane but on the volitional-emotional plane. Concepts such as joy, delight (arevut) and devotion (devekut) become central.
Stage C (the stratum of the "doctrine of love"): a late and mature synthesis in which the concept of "love" becomes the central cosmic and theological foundation, which organizes and unites all the parts of the system. The full correspondence between this stratum and the introduction to the book is further proof that it is the late, summarizing editorial stage of the work.
This developmental model, reconstructed here on the basis of the textual evidence, provides for the first time a coherent framework for understanding the tensions and conceptual leaps in Crescas's thought. Having established the existence of the "stratum of love" as a distinct and late textual layer, we can now turn with confidence to an in-depth analysis of its rich theological contents.
Part Two: The Theology of the "Stratum of Love": Love as the Central Axis of Crescas's Late Thought
This analysis will focus on the comprehensive theological system that emerges from the "stratum of love". We shall see how the idea of love is not exhausted by being a moral end or a personal religious experience, but functions as an overarching principle that organizes the whole of reality. For the late Crescas, love is the principle that constitutes God's relation to the world, the very act of creation, the nature of divine providence and the meaning of the Torah.
B.1. God as Lover: Breaking through Negative Theology
Crescas's first and decisive step in establishing his doctrine of love is the revolution he brings about in the conception of God. In order to be able to speak of "God's love", he had to break through the framework of negative theology laid down by Maimonides. The philosophical basis for this move is Crescas's "doctrine of essential attributes". According to it, although we cannot grasp God's infinite essence, we can ascribe to Him attributes that indicate something essential to Him, flowing from His essence. Thus, attributes such as "love" and "joy" express an essential truth about the manner of His action and His relation to the world.
On this basis, Crescas conducts a sharp polemic against the intellectual and impersonal conception of God of Jewish rationalism (Maimonides and Gersonides). In a brilliant stroke, he uses Gersonides' own arguments to expose the inconsistency of his system. Gersonides ascribed "joy" to God, but Crescas attacks this assertion and points to the contradiction: joy and love, he argues, belong to the faculty of will and imagination, which do not exist in a "pure intellect". An Aristotelian God can be an object of love, but cannot himself love.
Here Crescas's conceptual revolution takes place: divine love does not stem from lack or from desire (as in the Neoplatonic conception), but precisely from perfection, power and abundance. The perfect God is the ultimate lover, and His love is an expression of His perfection. Describing God as "loving" reconstitutes the religious relationship. Instead of an intellectualist ideal of intellectual cleaving to an abstract God, Crescas offers an emotional, personal and dialogical relationship with a personal, loving and rejoicing God.
B.2. Creation and Providence as an Expression of God's Love
In Crescas's teaching, God's love is not an abstract idea but an active and creative force. Its clearest expression is in the act of creation. Crescas develops an original conception of the continual "renewal of the world", based on the blessing "who in His goodness renews every day, continually, the work of creation". According to this conception, creation is not a one-time event that took place in the past, but an active and continuing act of love. God, out of His love and His will to do good, constantly "bestows" the existence of the world.
The conception of providence, too, is reinterpreted in the light of the principle of love. Crescas distinguishes between two types of providence:
General providence: This is a providence subject to natural and astrological law, which applies to the whole of creation and to the nations of the world.
Special providence: This is a direct and personal providence of love, reserved for the people of Israel. This providence is not subject to astral law, but stems directly from the relationship of mutual love between God and His people.
B.3. The Human Response: The Torah as a Path to Love
How did this special relationship between God and Israel come about? Crescas's answer boldly incorporates theological concepts drawn from the polemic with Christianity. He adopts the idea of "original sin" but gives it a distinctive interpretation: the sin is not a hereditary moral defect but the "inclination to materiality" that arose in humankind. Judaism, according to Crescas, is the path intended to free man from this inclination and enable him to realize his purpose – the love of God.
In this process, Abraham our father and the Torah play a founding role:
Abraham our father: Abraham, in his immense love for God, broke through the framework of general providence. His love, which was expressed in concrete deeds – the commandment of circumcision and his readiness for the sacrifice of the Binding (the Akedah) – created a unique and unprecedented interaction of love between God and his descendants, the people of Israel.
The Torah and its commandments: Since most human beings are not as perfect in their love as Abraham, the Torah was given to them. The commandments are not arbitrary laws but an educational instrument for refining the inclination to materiality and to lusts. They constitute a practical framework that enables a person to persevere in the service of love towards God.
This conception constitutes a twofold and sophisticated polemic. Inwardly, it sets up a "hasidic" ideal of love realized in deeds and in the fulfilment of commandments, against the intellectualist ideal. Outwardly, it argues against Christianity that true love does not abolish the commandments but requires them.
Understanding the rich theological structure of the doctrine of love now enables us to place it precisely in the historical and polemical context in which it grew.
Part Three: The Twofold Polemical Context of the "Doctrine of Love"
The development of the "doctrine of love" in Crescas's thought is not an abstract philosophical move. It is a direct, passionate and profound response to the spiritual and existential crises that befell his generation – the generation of the persecutions of 5151 (1391), a generation of forced apostasy, mass conversion and the undermining of the foundations of faith.
C.1. The Response to the Crisis of Jewish Rationalism
In the 14th century, the Jewish elites in Spain were deeply immersed in a culture of extreme philosophical rationalism, as scholars such as Yitzhak Baer and Dov Schwartz have shown. These currents tended to subordinate the beliefs of the Torah to universal philosophical truths, and thereby weakened faith in individual providence and the practical commitment to the commandments.
Crescas saw in this approach a fatal spiritual weakness. In his view, rationalism had emptied Judaism of its emotional, believing and living content, and turned it into a cold intellectual system. This weakness, he believed, was what prepared the ground for the spiritual collapse and the mass conversion that took place in the persecutions of 5151.
The "doctrine of love" is Crescas's attempt to offer a theological alternative. He sought to re-establish a Judaism that has emotional warmth, a personal relationship to God and an accessible existential meaning. It is a "popular" theology in the deep sense of the word – not simplistic, but one that addresses the human heart, both that of the masses and that of the hesitating intellectual, and offers it a firm spiritual anchor.
C.2. Internalization and Polemic vis-à-vis Christianity
The analysis of the "stratum of love" reveals a brilliant polemical method, in which Crescas does not reject Christian concepts out of hand but subjects them to a radical theological "conversion", as illustrated in the following key points:
Original sin: Crescas accepts the existence of original sin but defines it as the inclination to materiality. Atonement for it, he argues, lies not in faith in Jesus but in the fulfilment of the commandments, which refine the body.
The sacrifice: The act of the Binding of Isaac, and not the crucifixion of Jesus, is the sacrifice of love that establishes the special covenant between God and His people.
The new covenant: This is Abraham's covenant of circumcision, a covenant of practical love, and not the spiritual Christian covenant.
Love: The idea of love, which stands at the centre of Christian theology, undergoes a radical "conversion". It becomes a love realized and sustained through the commandments, in complete contrast to the "spiritual" Christian love, which, in Crescas's view, abolishes the commandments.
The depth of this polemic cannot be understood without recognizing the enormous influence of the apostate Abner of Burgos on the early stratum of Crescas's thought. As shown in Part One, Crescas adopted the rigid determinism from Abner. This adoption attests to the intellectual relations of "intimacy and hatred" that prevailed between the religions in this period, and to Crescas's willingness to draw truth even from the sources of his bitterest opponent.
Conclusion: Crescas's Spiritual Journey – from Determinism to Love
At the opening of our discussion we presented the book "Or Hashem" as a multifaceted work that developed in stages. Now, at the end of the analytical journey, we can summarize the findings of the study according to the presumed order of their historical development, and sketch the outlines of the spiritual and intellectual journey of Crescas himself.
The course of Crescas's thought, as reflected in the editorial layers of "Or Hashem", is a dramatic journey that begins with a rigid philosophical determinism and culminates in a cosmic theology of love.
The starting point: At the early stage, under the profound influence of Abner of Burgos, Crescas adopted a sharply deterministic conception. This move was a counter-reaction to the Jewish rationalism of his day, which, in its denial of individual providence, seemed to Crescas to undermine the foundations of faith.
The transitional stage: Gradually, as is evident in the "Passover Sermon" and in the parallel layers of "Or Hashem", Crescas began to move away from the intellectualist emphasis. He developed a conception that locates human choice not in the intellect but on the emotional-volitional plane – in a person's ability to rejoice in his faith and to feel delight (arevut) in the fulfilment of its commandments.
The peak: Finally, Crescas formulated the comprehensive and mature "doctrine of love". Here love is no longer merely a human emotion but becomes a central cosmic and theological principle. It is the cause of creation, the essence of providence, the purpose of the Torah and the summit to which man aspires.
Crescas's intellectual enterprise was a daring attempt to restore to Judaism its emotional and believing vitality in a period of deep existential crisis. He did so through a move of "restoring the crown to its former glory" – a return to root biblical ideas of mutual love between God and His people ("And you shall love the Lord your God...", "I have loved you with an everlasting love..."). But this was not a naive return; it was a sophisticated move that used the most up-to-date philosophical tools of his time and conducted a daring and original polemic with his opponents from within and from without.
Thus, this stratigraphic analysis does not merely solve textual difficulties; it reveals Crescas not only as a systematic philosopher but as a religious thinker struggling existentially for the vitality of Jewish faith at a critical moment in its history. The "doctrine of love", then, is not just an interesting chapter in his thought, but his theological, spiritual and existential answer to the tremendous challenges that confronted his generation. Understanding his spiritual journey from determinism to love is, therefore, a key to understanding one of the most dramatic junctures in Jewish thought.
The Philosophical-Scientific Thought of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas: The Influence of Abner of Burgos on the Critique of Aristotelian Physics
1. Introduction: Rabbi Hasdai Crescas as a Critic of Aristotelian Science
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (Rahak, 1340-1410) stands as one of the central and revolutionary figures in Jewish thought of the late Middle Ages. His strategic importance lies in the comprehensive and systematic critical campaign he waged against Aristotelian philosophy and physics, which had reigned supreme in Jewish, Christian and Muslim thought for hundreds of years. Whereas many thinkers before him had tried to reconcile the philosophical tradition with the religious tradition, Crescas chose to challenge the basic assumptions of Aristotelian science, and thereby opened the way to new scientific and philosophical thinking.
The central thesis of this document is that Crescas's sharp critique of basic concepts of Aristotelian physics, and in particular of the concepts of place and motion, did not grow in a vacuum. It was decisively influenced by the thought of a radical thinker who preceded him, the apostate rabbi Abner of Burgos (1270-1348), as emerges from the article by Shalom Sadik. This document isolates and clarifies this specific line of intellectual influence, in order to demonstrate in a focused way how radical ideas, which were almost entirely lost, found their way into the heart of the central Jewish philosophical critique. This influence was not confined to physics alone, but also touched deeper philosophical definitions, such as the definition of matter and the doctrine of human choice. To understand the depth of the revolution Crescas brought about and its sources, one must first examine the original ideas that Abner of Burgos put forward, ideas that were almost lost in the depths of history.
2. The Background to the Critique: The Scientific Thought of Abner of Burgos
Abner of Burgos was a thinker who proposed radical alternatives to the scientific conceptions of his time, even before he converted. Unfortunately, his principal scientific book, "Hitpalsefut he-Hadash" ("The New Philosophizing"), has been lost, and our knowledge of his scientific thought is based on the reconstruction of his ideas from his other surviving writings, chief among them "Moreh Tzedek" ("Teacher of Righteousness", written in Spanish after his conversion to Christianity) and "Sefer Meyasher Akov" ("The Book That Straightens the Crooked", written in Hebrew). From these writings emerges the picture of an original thinker who broke down the conceptual connections of the prevailing physics into their components.
2.1. A New Definition of "Place" and "Dimension"
One of Abner's central innovations was severing the essential connection between "dimension" and "body" (geshem). Whereas the Aristotelian conception saw dimension as an inseparable property of the physical body, Abner presented a revolutionary definition, according to which dimension is an independent entity:
"A simple quantity, bare and pure of all moving bodies"
This definition, which presents dimension as a pure quantity abstracted from any physical body, paves the way to recognizing the existence of a "void" – a space possessing dimensions that is not filled by a body. This move stands in complete contrast to the Aristotelian conception, which utterly denied the possibility of the existence of the void. On the basis of this separation, Abner drew an important distinction between two kinds of place:
Potential place: empty, "vacant" dimensions, ready to receive a body into them.
Actual place: the same dimensions when they are already filled by a body.
2.2. Severing the Connection between "Motion" and "Place"
Having severed dimension from body, Abner went on to sever the causal connection between "motion" and **"place"**. According to Aristotelian physics, natural motion (for example, that of a stone falling to the ground) is caused by the body's striving to reach its "natural place". Abner rejected this conception utterly. He argued that the final place to which the body moves is not an active factor in the motion but merely "a mark in the distance". That is, place is a passive reference point in space, and not an active end that draws the body towards it.
He sharpened this argument in Segulah 33 of "Sefer Meyasher Akov". There he argued that, contrary to the Aristotelian position, no moment of rest is required between two opposite motions (such as rising and falling). Since place is not the end that causes the motion, there is no reason for the body to stop at the turning point in order to "exhaust" its motion in one direction before it begins its motion in the opposite direction. These ideas, which dismantled the foundations of the Aristotelian explanation of motion, served as the groundwork for the in-depth critique that Rabbi Hasdai Crescas would develop in his wake.
3. Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's Critique of the Aristotelian Conception of Place
In his book "Or Hashem", Rabbi Hasdai Crescas adopts and develops Abner's lines of critique in order to undermine Aristotle's physics systematically. He uses Abner's ideas as a starting point for presenting an alternative conception of space and motion, one that stresses the separation between the concepts that Aristotle had bound together.
3.1. Defining Place as "Empty Space" (Panui)
Crescas's definition of place clearly echoes Abner's definition. He too sees place as an entity independent of the body, as emerges from his definition:
"It is the empty space equal to the body, which the body occupies"
Like Abner, the definition of place as "empty space" presupposes the possible existence of a void. Place is an empty space whose measurements are equal to the measurements of the body (the "geshem") that "occupies" it, that is, fills it temporarily. Crescas too adopts the distinction between two states of place:
Potential place: the empty space ready to receive the body.
Actual place: the empty space when the body already fills it.
3.2. Denying the Role of the "Surrounding" Body
Crescas's definition directly negates the famous Aristotelian definition of place – "the limit of the surrounding body". According to Aristotle, the place of an object is defined by the inner boundary of the body that envelops it. Crescas, by contrast, abolishes the dependence of place on external bodies. In his view, the empty dimensions themselves are what "surround", and therefore an object can be in a place even if it is in an absolute void, with no other body around it. This definition frees the concept of place from the shackles of the full physical world and turns it into an abstract concept of space. Having replaced Aristotelian "place" – a finite and qualitative entity – with an infinite and neutral "empty space", it was only to be expected that Crescas would go on to challenge its causal role as an end ("natural place") in the theory of motion. A place that is an infinite void can no longer serve as a final end.
4. Analysis of the Influence and Its Implications
The clear parallels uncovered between the thought of Abner of Burgos and that of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas point to a clear line of intellectual influence from one thinker to the other. This influence had far-reaching implications, both for the preservation of Abner's ideas and for the development of Jewish and scientific thought.
4.1. Comparison Table: Abner of Burgos and Crescas
The following table illustrates visually the main similarities between the two thinkers on the subjects of place and motion.
4.2. The Significance of the Historical Influence
Crescas's adoption of the ideas of Abner of Burgos is an extraordinary historical phenomenon. Abner was a deeply controversial figure in the Jewish world because of his conversion to Christianity, and it is reasonable to assume that his scientific writings, which were written in Hebrew before he converted, did not survive independently. Jews were wary of studying the books of the apostate, while Christians showed no interest in scientific writings composed in Hebrew. In this state of affairs, Rabbi Hasdai Crescas was in all likelihood the almost exclusive channel through which these radical scientific ideas passed. He not only preserved them but also absorbed them into the heart of Jewish philosophical discourse and made them an integral part of his critique of Aristotelianism.
4.3. Dismantling the Aristotelian System
Beyond its historical importance, the move made by Abner and Crescas had a profound philosophical implication. One of the great advantages of Aristotelian physics was its uniformity and coherence; all the concepts – matter, dimension, place, motion and end – were bound up with one another in a tight system of explanations. By systematically severing these connections, Abner and Crescas dismantled the monolithic structure of Aristotelian physics and exposed its weaknesses. They showed that each of the concepts could be thought of separately, and thereby opened the way to a more analytical scientific thinking, one not bound to a closed conceptual system. Whereas Aristotelian physics offered a teleological and aesthetic explanation of the world, in which everything has an end and a natural place, the move of Abner and Crescas replaced it with a more mechanistic model, in which space is a neutral arena for the forces acting within it. This is a decisive step, heralding the transition from medieval physics to the physics of the modern era.
Crescas thereby fulfilled a twofold and decisive role: he was both a preserver of the lost ideas of a rejected thinker and a revolutionary thinker who used these ideas to challenge the dominant philosophical tradition of his time.
5. Summary
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's trenchant and systematic critique of Aristotelian physics is not a creation out of nothing. As has been shown, his revolutionary ideas on the subjects of place and motion rest clearly on foundations laid some seventy years before him by the thinker Abner of Burgos. Crescas adopted, developed and integrated Abner's definitions of place as empty space and his severing of the causal connection between place and motion, and used them as a central tool in his attack on Aristotelian science. This intellectual move of Crescas, which combines the preservation of radical ideas with their development into a coherent critical system, is an important chapter not only in the history of Jewish thought but also in the history of science, as part of the broader trend of challenging and dismantling the Aristotelian paradigm in the late Middle Ages.
Love as a Founding Principle: Understanding Rabbi Hasdai Crescas's Doctrine of Love
1. Introduction: Why Love? Crescas's Revolution in a World of Crisis
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (Rahak, c. 1340-1410) was not only a brilliant philosopher but a spiritual leader who worked in one of the darkest periods of Spanish Jewry. He lived and worked at the time of the persecutions of 5151 (1391), terrible persecutions that led to mass conversion and a deep crisis of faith. In response to the crisis, Crescas offered an answer that was not merely political but theological and philosophical. He placed at the centre of Jewish thought one founding principle, simple and powerful: love.
Crescas's answer was a spiritual and intellectual counter-attack on two fronts: against the cold and elitist philosophy of his Jewish predecessors, and against the growing theological pressure of the Christian world around him.
As the scholar S. B. Urbach put it: "Love is the key to Crescas's entire system; the mutual relationship of God to man and of man to God... everything is determined by love."
To understand the magnitude of Crescas's innovation, we must glance for a moment at the world of thought that preceded him.
2. The Background: A World without Love? The God of the Philosophers before Crescas
Before Crescas, Jewish thought was deeply influenced by the rationalist philosophy of Maimonides and Gersonides. This conception saw God as a perfect, abstract and impersonal intellectual being – "intellect, intellecting subject and intellected object" – who is not described in terms of emotion or will. The way to reach such a God was intellectual, and was intended for a small philosophical elite.
Crescas proposed a radical alternative, far more accessible and personal.
The rationalist conception created distance and a sense that the bond with God was reserved for a select few. Crescas, by contrast, sought to offer a path open to every person – the path of the heart.
How, then, did Crescas succeed in presenting so different a conception of God, and what is the meaning of "the love of God"?
3. Crescas's Solution: A God Who Loves and Wills the Good
The great challenge that faced Crescas was how one could ascribe to an infinite and perfect God a "human" quality such as love. The philosophers before him had denied this utterly. Crescas's solution was the development of a doctrine of "essential attributes". According to this conception:
Not an emotion but an action: God's love is not an emotion of being affected or a passing feeling (passivity), but an active and constant action of the will to do good, to give and to bestow good upon the world.
His actions can be known: We cannot understand God's absolute essence, but we can know His attributes – that is, His ways of acting in the world. Love, joy and will are descriptions of divine actions that we can grasp. God's joy, for example, is not a passive emotion that stems from knowledge, but an active action of giving, as it is said: "The Lord shall rejoice in His works" – that is, He rejoices in the very act of creation and of His constant beneficence.
Love stems from perfection: Contrary to the view that love stems from lack or need, Crescas argued that it stems precisely from perfection and power. The more perfect and stronger the lover, the greater his love. Since God is the source of perfection, He is necessarily the ultimate lover.
How is this immense love expressed in our everyday reality?
4. Love in Action: Continuous Creation and Personal Providence
Crescas identified two central expressions of God's love acting in the world:
Creation as a continuing act of love: The world was not created once and left to itself. According to Crescas, God's love is so great that He creates and brings reality into being anew at every single moment. This idea rests on what we know from the prayer book: "who in His goodness renews every day, continually, the work of creation". Creation is not a historical event but a dynamic process of unceasing abundance and love.
Providence as an expression of caring: Divine providence is not an indifferent law of nature but a "providence of love". Crescas distinguishes between a general providence over the whole world (which stems from the very fact of continuous creation) and a more special and personal providence over the people of Israel. This providence stems from the mutual relationship of love between Israel and its God, a relationship sealed in a covenant of deed and love.
If God loves the world, what is our own role in this relationship?
5. The Purpose of Man: To Answer Love with Love
Sharply and clearly, Crescas determines that the supreme purpose of man is one: to love God. He did not invent this idea, but returned it to centre stage, basing it on the most central commandment in the Torah.
"And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might" (Deuteronomy 6:5)
For Crescas, this is not an abstract or intellectual-philosophical love. It is a practical, emotional love that encompasses a person's entire being – his heart, his soul and his deeds.
But how, in practice, can a person develop and express so great a love? Here the decisive role of the commandments comes in.
6. The Path to Love: The True Purpose of the Commandments
Crescas proposed a revolutionary conception of the purpose of the commandments, contrary to what was accepted in the philosophical and Christian circles of his generation. In his view, the commandments are the practical path to attaining the love of God.
Not an intellectual aim: The commandments are not merely a tool for attaining intellectual perfection, as the rationalists claimed.
An instrument for purifying the soul: And in a daring and surprising move, Crescas took one of the most powerful tools of his theological opponents and made it his own. He adopted the concept of "the taint of original sin" from the Christian world, but redefined it in a radically Jewish way. For him, it is not a metaphysical sin erased by faith, but an "inclination to materiality" inherent in man. The main aim of the commandments is to refine this inclination, to purify the soul, and thereby to clear room in it to be filled with the pure love of God.
Perseverance in love: The multitude of commandments is not a burden but an opportunity. It is intended to enable a person to engage in the love of God constantly, daily and continuously, and to make love an inseparable part of his life, and not merely an abstract idea.
This conception posed a twofold challenge: it opposed the rationalists, who saw the commandments as a means of intellectual perfection, and at the same time offered a strong Jewish alternative to Christianity, which had abolished most of the practical commandments in favour of spiritual faith.
Now, having understood both sides – God's love and man's love – we can see how they combine into a continuing cosmic dialogue.
7. Summary: Crescas's Legacy – A Religion of Bond and Love
The teaching of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas constituted a quiet and profound revolution in Jewish thought. His legacy can be summarized in three central points:
The alternative to rationalism: Crescas set up a religious conception that is personal, emotional and accessible to every person, against the elitist and remote philosophy that had prevailed before him. He brought religious experience back from the intellect to the heart.
Love as a unifying principle: For Crescas, love is not merely an emotion or a secondary commandment, but the organizing principle that explains everything: the creation of the world, divine providence, the purpose of the Torah and the aim of human life.
A Judaism of deed and polemic: He reconnected the world of deed with the world of the spirit, and stressed that the path to the love of God passes through the fulfilment of the practical commandments. He thereby created a new Jewish synthesis, by adopting and "converting" Christian ideas (such as love and original sin) in order to struggle both against Christian influence and against the weakness of Jewish rationalism.
Today, too, Crescas's teaching resonates powerfully, and is a source of inspiration for anyone seeking a living, personal and meaningful bond with God.

Rabbi Hasdai Crescas: A Theological, Cosmological and Scientific Revolution
This survey sketches the outlines of the figure of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas, a daring spiritual and political leader who was active in 14th-century Spain and set up a revolutionary alternative to Aristotelian rationalism. The text presents his many-sided activity, from the rehabilitation of Jewish communities after the persecutions of 5151 to the writing of his monumental work "Or Hashem", in which he dismantled ancient physical and metaphysical assumptions. His thought is highlighted as having paved a new path in the fields of space, time and free choice, while shifting the religious centre of gravity from cold intellect towards emotion, intention and the love of God. Crescas's importance is presented not only in the internal Jewish context but also as that of a pioneer who anticipated modern science and deeply influenced central Western philosophers such as Spinoza and Kant.
The Activity, Torah Teaching and Philosophical Influence of Rabbi Hasdai Crescas: A Theological, Cosmological and Scientific Revolution
Introduction: Spiritual and Political Leadership in an Era of Change and Crisis
Rabbi Hasdai bar Avraham Crescas (acronym: Rahak; c. 1340 – 1411) represents one of the most original, daring and influential peaks in the history of Jewish philosophy and scientific thought of the late Middle Ages.[1, 2] Crescas was active in a historical period saturated with profound upheavals for the Jewry of the Iberian Peninsula, which reached their bitter and violent climax in the persecutions of 5151 (1391).[1, 3] In the midst of this existential crisis, he revealed himself not only as a thinker of exceptional intellectual freedom but also as a dominant political and diplomatic leader, an authorized rabbinic judge and a distinguished halakhist, who directed with a strong hand the rehabilitation of the ruined communities in the Kingdom of Aragon.[1, 2, 4] His Torah and philosophical teaching, which undermined the foundations of the extreme Aristotelian rationalism that prevailed in his time, presented a comprehensive intellectual alternative whose influences resonated hundreds of years later and left an indelible mark on the thinkers of the modern era, foremost among them Baruch Spinoza and Immanuel Kant.[5, 6]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Historical Biography and a Chronology of Leadership
Crescas was born in Barcelona in the Principality of Catalonia, under the Crown of Aragon, to a distinguished family of Torah scholars.[1, 4] His father, Rabbi Avraham ben Rabbi Hasdai Crescas (the Elder), was a prominent Spanish rabbi and the teacher of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Sheshet (the Rivash).[1] Crescas acquired most of his Torah from the greatest scholar of the generation at that time, Rabbi Nissim ben Reuven (the Ran), in whose study house learning was not limited to halakhic study alone but combined with in-depth engagement in philosophy, political science and metaphysics.[1] In that intellectual environment a strong bond was formed between Crescas and his friend the Rivash, who studied Torah from Crescas himself as well, alongside his studies with the Ran and Rabbi Peretz ha-Kohen.[1, 4, 7]
Crescas's life moved ceaselessly between the walls of the study house and the corridors of royal power.[1, 5] He conducted far-flung business in precious stones, luxury goods and animals, commanded the Romance languages, Catalan and Aragonese, and served at the royal court as a legal adviser, translator and intermediary.[1] Despite his high public standing, in the year 5127 (1378) Crescas was imprisoned together with the Ran, the Rivash and other leaders of the Barcelona community following a false accusation and internal informing.[1, 4] After his release he returned to vigorous political activity, and in the year 5143 (1383) he conducted complex negotiations with King Pedro IV of Catalonia concerning the rights of the Jews.[1] Later he drew close to King Juan I and Queen Violant of Aragon, and received the royal title "member of the royal household".[1, 5]
The year 1391 (the persecutions of 5151) marked the greatest personal and national rupture of his life.[1, 3] During the cruel massacre of the Jews of Barcelona, his only son was killed, a young bridegroom of about twenty.[1, 8] Crescas accepted the judgment with perfect faith, and in a historic letter that he sent to the community of Avignon in France to describe the dimensions of the national catastrophe, he wrote of the loss of his son the words: "I offered him up as a burnt offering, an unblemished lamb; I will accept the judgment upon me as just, and take comfort in the goodness of his portion".[1, 8] After the riots Crescas left ruined Barcelona and moved to Saragossa, where he had already been appointed rabbi of the community, with royal approval, in 1388.[1, 5] In Saragossa he in fact sat in the seat of his friend the Rivash, who had left Spain for Algiers in the wake of the persecutions.[7, 8] In Saragossa Crescas established a splendid yeshiva that attracted important Torah scholars, among them Rabbi Yosef Albo (author of "Sefer ha-Ikkarim", "The Book of Principles") and Rabbi Yosef Chaviva (author of "Nimmukei Yosef").[1, 4, 8] Alongside their engagement in settled halakha, the students of the yeshiva engaged in systematic philosophical thought under the guidance of their teacher.[8]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Halakhic Enterprise and the Synthesis of the Commandments: From "Ner Elohim" to the "Passover Sermon"
Alongside his image as a revolutionary philosopher, Crescas was first and foremost a halakhist of great stature, to whom halakhic questions and treatises were addressed from all over Spain.[1, 8] Crescas's attitude to halakha and to the Oral Torah was one of absolute commitment, and he saw in them the supreme source of the spiritual life of the nation.[11] His close halakhic ties with his friend the Rivash found expression in extensive correspondence, part of which was preserved and printed in the responsa books of the period, such as the famous letter from Crescas to the Rivash that appears as section 269 in the Responsa of the Rivash.[8] This bond attests to the joint activity of the two in the legal and Torah leadership of Spanish Jewry, despite the theological differences of outlook between them, such as the Rivash's complex and reserved attitude to practical Kabbalah and to engaging in it when it had not been received from an authorized teacher, as expressed in the Responsa of the Rivash, section 157.[7]
Crescas's halakhic conception strove to create an innovative and wide-ranging halakhic code that was to be called "Ner Elohim" ("The Lamp of God").[1] This master plan was intended to present the commandments of the Torah with their causes and reasons according to their subject matter, while explaining the commandments meticulously and noting their direct connections to the Talmudic sources.[1] According to Crescas's vision, the book "Or Hashem" was to serve only as the first part of this monumental enterprise, and its purpose was to define the foundations of faith and of theological philosophy that would serve as the conceptual substrate for the entire halakhic system.[1] Although this plan as a whole was not carried out because of the circumstances of the time and the tribulations of his life, the core of the halakhic and intellectual part merged into his philosophical work.[1]
Further evidence of his Torah activity, which combined halakha and philosophy, is the "Passover Sermon" that he composed.[1, 8] This sermon, which opens with the words familiar from the Mishnah, "On the night of the fourteenth [of Nisan] one searches for leaven by the light of a candle", is a profound philosophical and theological discourse that uses the laws of searching for leaven and the laws of the festival as a basis for a discussion of the nature of physical and spiritual light, the role of the intellect in apprehending the intelligibles, and the relation of the soul to God.[8] The sermon, which was first printed in the journal "He-Halutz" (year 7, p. 93), faithfully reflects the way in which Crescas did not separate the operative halakhic world from abstract philosophical speculation, but saw them as two sides of the same coin, nourishing each other.[8]
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The Book "Or Hashem": Methodical Structure and Intellectual Architecture
The book "Or Hashem" represents a meticulous logical-architectonic structure, carefully designed to serve as a systematic alternative to the theological structure of Maimonides' "Guide of the Perplexed".[8, 9] Crescas chose to divide his book into four main treatises, each devoted to a different level of categorization of Jewish beliefs: the roots, the cornerstones, the obligatory beliefs, and the rational speculations.[9, 10] This division is not merely technical; it is intended to clarify which principles are those without which the religion of Moses cannot exist at all, and which principles, though part of the Torah tradition, are not a necessary condition for the very definition of Jewish faith.[5, 9]
The method Crescas adopts is characterized by the use of distinctly philosophical and scholastic tools, drawing both on the Jewish tradition and on the Latin translations of medieval thought.[12] He makes precise use of metaphysical terms such as substance, essence, attribute and cause, in order to examine the validity of the Aristotelian basic assumptions.[12] The first proofread critical edition of the book, based on ancient manuscripts such as Florence, Laurenziana manuscript 417, appeared only in 5750 (1990), edited by Rabbi Shlomo Fisher, and thereby opened the way to in-depth modern research into the methodical structure of the work.[8, 13]

Breaking Aristotelian Physics: Space, Time, Infinity and Matter
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas is considered one of the most revolutionary cosmologists and physicists of the period of the Rishonim, and he was the first to dare to cast systematic and sweeping doubt on Aristotle's physical determinations, which were considered at that time to be absolute scientific truths not to be questioned.[1, 2] Aristotle had shaped a closed, limited and finite cosmos, in which every motion is conditional on direct physical contact, empty space is impossible, and time is an accidental phenomenon wholly dependent on the motion of matter in space.[6, 14] Crescas dismantled this picture by means of a series of brilliant scientific and metaphysical objections, which were developed in the modern era by the greatest physicists and philosophers.[1, 6]
The Concept of Empty Space (the Vacuum) and Its Existential Implications
Aristotle utterly denied the existence of a void (vacuum) in reality, and argued that space is always filled with some physical matter.[6, 14] Crescas rejected this position utterly and proved that the existence of an unlimited empty space is not only logically possible but necessary.[6, 14]
In a modern analysis of his thought, as presented in Rav Shagar's lectures on the book "Or Hashem", it is revealed that Crescas's revolution in physics carries profound theological and existential implications.[14] The fact that physical being is located within an open and empty space creates the realm of possibility, of doubt and of searching.[14] The cosmic void is the substrate that makes possible human freedom and the soul's constant pursuit of the unattainable absolute, in contrast to the closed and alienated Aristotelian cosmos, in which every body is locked into its predetermined natural place.[14]
The Question of Actual Infinity and the Plurality of Worlds
Maimonides' third premise, based on Aristotle, denied the possibility of the existence of an infinite causal chain or of an actually infinite physical magnitude.[14] Crescas attacked this assumption and proved that the concept of actual infinity is entirely consistent.[6]
The universe is not bounded by an outermost sphere beyond which absolute "nothing" reigns (as Aristotle held, identifying the world with the fifth element – the ether).[6] The universe as a whole can be infinite in its dimensions, and from this follows the daring conclusion, in the second speculation of the fourth treatise, that infinitely many worlds may exist in infinite space.[6, 9]
The Definition of Place and Time outside Matter
Aristotle defined "place" as the surrounding boundary of the surrounded body.[6, 14] Crescas rejected this relative definition and defined place as the empty three-dimensional space itself, which exists in its own right, independently of the bodies that occupy it.[14]
Similarly, Crescas dismantled Aristotle's definition of time as the measure of the motion of physical bodies.[6, 14] Crescas argued that time can be measured even in a state of absolute rest, and defined time as "the measure of the continuity of motion or of rest between two instants".[6] Time, in his view, is an independent intellectual-psychological phenomenon ("the existence of time is in the soul") that is not conditional on the existence of physical bodies in reality.[6]
Matter and Form and Cosmic Alienation
Maimonides' tenth premise states that every corporeal body is composed of matter and form.[14] Rav Shagar's analysis makes clear that for Aristotle and Maimonides matter was always perceived as an external, alienated and negative object, which prevents man from reaching metaphysical perfection and absolute divine unity.[14] Crescas sought to bridge this gap and bring material reality closer to the divine, by freeing physics from the oppressive dualistic composition of matter and form and by identifying matter as an integral part of the divine will that sustains the world at every moment.[4, 14]

The Metaphysics of the Will: Knowledge, Choice and the Doctrine of Attributes
At the centre of Crescas's theological teaching stands a systematic and daring attempt to grapple with some of the greatest difficulties of religious philosophy: the relation between God's knowledge and free choice, and the doctrine of the divine attributes.[4, 13] Crescas's solutions to these questions establish an innovative position that distinguishes between objective reality and subjective experience.[4]
The Metaphysics of Possibility and Creation
Crescas starts from the definition of the essence of creation: the creation of the world "ex nihilo" (yesh me-ayin) means that God is the cause of all particulars, both as regards their form and as regards their content.[13] From this it necessarily follows that God knows all the particulars, every one of them, with complete and absolute knowledge.[13]
In discussing the metaphysical category of "the possible", which stands between "nothing" (absolute nullity) and "being" (complete necessity and obligation), Crescas determines that "the nature of the possible exists".[4, 13] The existence of the possible in the world follows from two distinct points of view: on the one hand, from the point of view of creation, there is full divine providence and knowledge of particulars on the part of the Creator; on the other hand, from the point of view of the Creator's freedom to create as He wills, the world is fundamentally "possible" (and not necessary, as Aristotle, who believed in the eternity of the world, held), and from this it follows that freedom of choice exists in the world.[13]
Solving the Difficulty of Knowledge and Choice: Practical Determinism and Freedom of Intention
The great difficulty that occupied Crescas's predecessors was how God's foreknowledge does not abolish free choice.[4] Gersonides resolved it by arguing that God knows all the possibilities but does not know which of them will actually be realized, whereas Maimonides left this question as an insoluble mystery lying beyond the grasp of the human intellect.[4] Crescas rejects both systems and determines that the question can be understood rationally.[4] In his view, God knows with complete and absolute knowledge all the deeds that will be done and the exact way in which matters will be decided.[4]
Crescas presents a solution based on a sharp distinction between two levels of human existence [4]:
The level of objective action (absolute determinism): The physical deeds that actually occur in the world are absolutely necessary and are determined by a chain of causes leading directly to the divine decision.[4] On the physical plane, man has no essential share in this determination and cannot change anything of what has been decreed in advance.[4]
The level of subjective intention and will (freedom of the will): The only realm left to man, in which his free choice applies, is the realm of intention, of the soul's inclination and of inner will.[4] The religious and moral question is not "what did you actually do" (since the deed was determined in advance), but "what was your intention in the deed you did".[4]
According to Crescas, divine judgment, assessment and governance are based on a person's relation to the deed and not on its physical product.[4] For Crescas there is no "test of outcome" but only a "test of intention".[4] The reward and punishment of the commandments are determined not by the external deed but by the intention and the inclination of the soul that accompany it.[4] From this follows Crescas's daring definition of the essence of reward and punishment: unlike Maimonides, who sees them as an external or intellectual recompense, Crescas argues that reward and punishment are a necessary and natural consequence embedded in the laws of divine creation (just as bodily harm is caused naturally by touching fire).[1] The word "u-vaharta" ("and you shall choose") refers, then, to a person's subjective sense of choice and to the inner will that he feels while performing the deed.[1]
The Doctrine of Positive Attributes and the Replacement of the Intellect by the Heart
Maimonides and Aristotle based their theology on an absolute negation of positive attributes of God (negative theology), out of fear that the ascription of positive attributes would impair the simple unity of the Creator.[8] Crescas rejected this approach and argued that positive essential attributes can be ascribed to God, such as goodness, loving-kindness and love, which do not impair His unity but flow from His infinite essence.[4, 8]
This turn changes completely the purpose of human existence: whereas Maimonides saw the perfection of human reason and conceptual cognition as the foundation of existence and of cleaving to God, Crescas placed devotion, awe and love at the centre.[4] The divine presence is attained not through a cold negation of attributes and intellectual abstraction, but through the fullness of religious experience, the understanding of the heart, the soul's own bonding and its full identification with the divine will.[4]

The Anti-Christian Polemic as an Enterprise of National Defence
In the wake of the persecutions of 5151 and the increasing theological and missionary pressure of the Christian Church on the remaining Jewish communities and on the masses of conversos (anusim) in Spain, Crescas saw an urgent need to equip himself with intellectual tools that would make it possible to confront the Christian claims logically on equal terms.[1, 3] To this end he composed in 1398 "Sefer Bittul Ikkarei ha-Notzrim" ("The Refutation of the Christian Principles").[1] The book was originally written in the Catalan language, to make possible direct public and internal debate with Christian scholars and conversos, and was translated into Hebrew in the year 5211 (1451) by the philosopher Rabbi Yosef ben Shem Tov.[1, 8]
In this work Crescas adopts a rigorous philosophical methodology based on the systematic logical dismantling of ten Christian articles of faith (among them: original sin, redemption, the Holy Trinity, the incarnation, the virgin birth, and transubstantiation).[1] Crescas's method of argument rests on two main foundations:
Textual analysis of the New Testament: Crescas examines the Christian scriptures and points to grave internal contradictions within them.[1] He uses simple logical tools to refute the metaphysical concepts of Christianity; thus, for example, he argues that if Jesus "the Son" was born of the Father, "God", and is entirely like Him, then the Father too was born, and if the Father was born, then He is caused and effected, which refutes His being divine and independent.[1]
Subjection to the laws of philosophical logic in the manner of Averroes (Ibn Rushd): Crescas bases his arguments on the determination of the Muslim philosopher Averroes (Ibn Rushd), according to which a religion can be considered legitimate only when its principles do not stand in absolute contradiction to general philosophical and logical reasoning.[1] Since Christianity presents principles (such as the Trinity or the transformation of the bread and wine into the flesh of God) that contradict the laws of common sense, it cannot be considered a legitimate religion.[1]
Scholars are divided as to the main target audience of the work [1]: the historian Zvi (Heinrich) Graetz held that the book was intended for Christian scholars who sought to understand why the Jews were unwilling to convert.[1] By contrast, the scholars Benzion Netanyahu and Daniel Lasker argue that it is an internal explanatory enterprise intended for Jews who stood on the verge of conversion or for conversos who sought to return to Judaism, with the aim of exposing to them the logical failings of the new religion and strengthening their loyalty to the Torah of Moses.[1]

Ripples of Influence on Modern Philosophy: From Spinoza to Kant
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas concludes the series of the great original systems of medieval Spanish Jewish philosophy, but his teaching served as a valuable theological and scientific bridge that connected scholastic thought with the modern thought of the new era.[5, 11] His main influences are evident chiefly in two of the most important Western philosophers: Baruch Spinoza and Immanuel Kant.[5, 6]
Crescas's Influence on Baruch Spinoza and the Doctrine of Substance
Baruch Spinoza knew Crescas's writings well, and in particular his discussions of infinity and its relation to God in the book "Or Hashem".[12] Spinoza used Crescas's proof of God as a valid model and illustrated some of his own basic assumptions by means of it.[12]
In analyzing the relationship between the two, as emerges from Avishai Galili's studies on the role of the intellect in the definition of the attribute according to Spinoza and its relation to Crescas's conception of essential attributes, several deep channels of influence can be identified [1]:
Infinity and the extension of space: Crescas determined that empty space is actually infinite and that God is not separate from place in the physical sense, but rather the whole of space is contained within Him.[6] Spinoza took this idea to a distinctly pantheistic extreme, and defined space (extension) as one of the two infinite attributes of the divine substance known to us ("God or Nature").[12]
Determinism and necessary causality: Crescas's deterministic view, according to which physical deeds are absolutely necessary and are determined by a fixed divine causal chain, served as the basis for Spinoza's doctrine of absolute determinism.[4] However, Spinoza abolished Crescas's distinction between deed and intention and denied freedom of the will completely.[1, 4]
The concept of substance and the attributes: the use of the scholastic terms (substance, essence, attribute, cause) that were shared by Crescas, Descartes and Spinoza.[12] Whereas Descartes was forced to express himself cautiously vis-à-vis the religious and ecclesiastical establishment because of the show trials of the opponents of the scientific method in his time, Spinoza presented an independent system that sought to subordinate religion to the state – a conception that relied on the Dutch model but whose metaphysical roots drew directly on Crescas's dismantling of the attributes.[12]
Anticipating Immanuel Kant's Epistemological Revolution
Crescas's thought anticipated by some three hundred years Immanuel Kant's "Copernican revolution" in the fields of epistemology and physics.[1, 6] Crescas's epistemological determination that "existing objects are apprehended not according to their nature – the nature of the existents – but according to the nature of the one who apprehends" is an early and precise formulation of Kant's distinction between "the thing in itself" (the noumena) and the thing as it is perceived by our mind (the phenomena).[1]
Moreover, Crescas's definition of time as an intellectual-psychological dimension that does not depend on matter and physical bodies ("the existence of time is in the soul") is entirely parallel to Kant's determination in his work "Critique of Pure Reason", according to which time is not an objective property of things but an a priori form of intuition of human consciousness.[6]

Summary and Conclusions
Rabbi Hasdai Crescas appears in Jewish and general history as an intellectual giant who united in his personality two rare qualities: courageous practical leadership in times of destruction and crisis, and a daring freedom of thought that does not shrink from breaking sacred scientific and philosophical paradigms.[1, 2, 3] His Torah teaching, as expressed in the book "Or Hashem", succeeded in rescuing Jewish faith from the intellectual stagnation of extreme rationalism, and returned to the centre of the religious stage the world of emotion, will, the heart and love, without giving up rigorous logical and scientific precision.[4, 10]
His scientific importance as a cosmologist and physicist of the first rank who presented an alternative to Aristotle's physics, together with his decisive influence on the shaping of Spinoza's metaphysics and Kant's epistemology, place him not only among the greatest sages of Israel of all generations, but among the fathers of modern thought and of the scientific revolution of the new era.[1, 5, 6] In historical perspective, Crescas's work proved that precisely from the depths of rupture and national destruction an independent, daring and liberating philosophical thought can grow, illuminating the path of the Jewish people and of the world of science for generations to come.[1, 3]
